task_row_model.query: For a patient with a prosthetic knee who is allergic to penicillin and needs a dental extraction, in which situations is antibiotic prophylaxis indicated and what preprocedural antibiotic and dose should be given for penicillin-allergic patients?

documents.content: Clinical guideline excerpts: Routine dental procedures do not require antibiotic prophylaxis for most patients with prosthetic joints. Prophylaxis is recommended only for high-risk subgroups: patients who are immunocompromised (for example, on chemotherapy or high-dose corticosteroids), those with a prior prosthetic joint infection, and patients within the early postoperative period after arthroplasty. The guideline specifies a single preprocedural oral dose for those indicated: amoxicillin 2 g administered 30–60 minutes before the dental procedure. The guidance emphasizes limiting prophylaxis to these risk categories to reduce unnecessary antibiotic exposure and resistance.
documents.reasoning_trace: Extracted criteria for which prosthetic joint patients need prophylaxis (immunocompromised, prior PJI, early post-op) and the non-allergic regimen (amoxicillin 2 g, 30–60 minutes preprocedure).

documents.content: Pharmacology and allergy management note: In patients with immediate-type penicillin hypersensitivity, preferred alternatives to aminopenicillins for dental prophylaxis are clindamycin and tetracyclines. Recommended oral dosing for prophylaxis against bacteremia from dental procedures is clindamycin 600 mg given 30–60 minutes before the procedure. If clindamycin is contraindicated (for example, recent C. difficile infection or intolerance), oral doxycycline 100 mg given approximately one hour before the procedure has been used as an alternative. Cephalosporins carry a low but nonzero cross-reactivity risk and are generally avoided in patients with a history of severe penicillin allergy.
documents.reasoning_trace: Provides penicillin-allergic alternative regimens and timing: clindamycin 600 mg 30–60 minutes prior, doxycycline 100 mg as alternative; cautions about cephalosporin cross-reactivity.

documents.content: Health news feature and historical perspective: For decades dentists and orthopedists debated whether dental work raises the already-low absolute risk of prosthetic joint infection. Media summaries often cite variable study results and small case reports; some older observational series report very low rates of hematogenous joint infection after dental procedures. Articles include unrelated case vignettes of infection after traumatic injuries and statistics about overall antibiotic prescribing trends in dentistry, with commentary on antibiotic stewardship and the history of prophylaxis policies dating back to the 1970s. These narratives reiterate controversy but do not provide specific dosing recommendations.
documents.reasoning_trace: Provides contextual, historical and statistical noise about controversy and low incidence; no additional actionable dosage or indication details for prophylaxis.

task_row_model.golden_answer: Antibiotic prophylaxis for dental extraction in a patient with a prosthetic knee is indicated only for high-risk patients: those who are immunocompromised, have had a prior prosthetic joint infection, or are in the early postoperative period after arthroplasty. For penicillin-allergic patients give oral clindamycin 600 mg 30–60 minutes before the procedure; if clindamycin is contraindicated, oral doxycycline 100 mg about one hour beforehand may be used.
